items.page: Probability Axioms: Foundation of Probability Theory
items.caption: The 36 outcomes of two dice, each with probability 1/36
items.text: Every cell is one outcome and carries the same non-negative weight, 1/36, so no probability is negative; the 36 weights add to exactly 1, which is the normalization axiom; and any event made of separate cells has probability equal to its count of cells over 36, which is additivity for disjoint outcomes. All three axioms are visible in one grid. Highlight an event and count its cells on the

items.caption: Branches below A carry P(B given A) and P(not B given A)
items.text: Bayes theorem rearranges two ways of reaching the same leaf: along the upper path the joint probability is P(A) times P(B given A), and the same leaf is reached the other way round through P(B) times P(A given B). Equating the two products and dividing by P(B) is the whole theorem. Change the branch weights and watch both products stay equal on the

items.text: The denominator P(B) collects the highlighted outcome from every branch: each branch contributes P(A<sub>i</sub>) times P(B given A<sub>i</sub>), and the sum of those contributions is the total probability of B. items.text: Here the cumulative probability rises without any jumps: probability is spread over intervals, so P(X = x) is zero for every single point and the curve climbs smoothly from 0 toward 1. items.secTitle: Using the CDF to Compute Probabilities
items.caption: Continuous uniform CDF, a = 0, b = 10: a straight ramp
items.text: For a uniform variable the CDF is a straight line from 0 at a to 1 at b, so the probability of any interval inside [a, b] is the difference of the two ramp heights, which is the length of the interval divided by b minus a. The difference F(b) minus F(a) is the same calculation on every distribution, only the curve changes. Pick two points and read the difference on the

items.page: Central Limit Theorem: Sample Means and Normal Distribution
items.caption: The standard normal density, the limit shape of averages
items.text: The bell curve is the destination of the theorem: whatever shape the original distribution has, the standardised sample mean approaches this density as the sample size grows. items.page: Combinatorics in Probability: Counting and Classical Formula
items.caption: Sum equals 7: six of the 36 equally likely cells
items.text: The classical formula counts cells: the event has six outcomes, the sample space has 36, so its probability is 6 over 36. items.caption: Given A: only the subtree below A remains
items.text: Once A is known to have occurred, the lower branch is discarded and the two branches below A are the whole remaining world. Their weights, P(B given A) and its complement, already add to 1, which is exactly what a conditional probability is: the probabilities inside the restricted situation. items.caption: Two events A and B with their intersection selected
items.text: Events behave as sets because they are sets of outcomes: the selected overlap is A and B, the two circles together are A or B, and everything outside a circle is its complement. The four regions of the diagram partition the sample space. Click a region and read its probability on the

items.page: Events in Probability: Sample Space and Event Operations
items.caption: Given A: the subtree below A
items.text: Assuming A has occurred discards the lower branch and leaves only the subtree below A, whose branch weights already sum to 1. The conditional probability of B is the weight of the B branch inside that subtree. Adjust the weights and watch the subtree renormalise on the

items.caption: A distribution pulled to the right: the mean follows the weight
items.text: The expected value is a balance point: values with more probability pull it toward them, so when the heavy bars sit on the right the marked mean moves right of the simple average of the values. Long-run averages of repeated draws settle at that balance point. Drag the weights and watch the mean shift on the

items.caption: A discrete distribution with E[X] = 3.4
items.text: Each value contributes its value times its probability, and the bars here add up to an expected value of 3.4. Moving one slider changes one probability and renormalises the rest, so the mean moves toward whichever value gained weight. Drag a slider and watch the sum update on the

items.caption: A waffle chart with equal columns: independence
items.text: Each column is a value of one variable and the shaded share in every column is the same: knowing the column tells you nothing about the shading, which is what independence looks like. Unequal shares across columns would mean dependence. Drag the shares apart and watch the events become dependent on the

items.caption: A 2 by 2 contingency table
items.text: Independence is a check on the table: the cell for A and B must equal the product of the row total and the column total, divided by the grand total. Disjoint events fail that check badly, because their shared cell is zero while the product is not, so disjoint and independent are opposite situations. Edit the cells and test the product rule on the

items.page: Law of Large Numbers: Sample Mean Convergence
items.caption: Standard normal density: the shape the central limit theorem adds
items.text: The law of large numbers says the sample mean settles at a single value; the central limit theorem adds the shape of the remaining fluctuation around that value, this bell curve, once the deviations are scaled up by the square root of n. Without the scaling the bell would shrink to a spike, which is the law itself. Compare the bell with other density shapes on the

items.caption: Exponential CDF, lambda = 1: the median is where F crosses one half
items.text: For a continuous variable the CDF is a smooth increasing curve, so it crosses one half at exactly one point; for the exponential family that point is the natural logarithm of 2 over lambda, about 0.69, well below the mean of 1 because of the right tail. Move along the curve and find where the accumulated probability reaches one half on the

items.caption: Normal CDF, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: Finding a continuous median means solving F(m) equal to one half; for a symmetric density such as the normal the solution is the centre of symmetry, here 0, where the S-curve passes through one half. Skewed families put the median away from the mean. Read the crossing point on the

items.caption: Poisson PMF, lambda = 3: two bars tie for the peak
items.text: The mode of a discrete distribution is the value under the tallest bar; for the Poisson family with an integer lambda the bars at lambda minus 1 and lambda are equally tall, so the distribution has two modes, 2 and 3. Change lambda to a non-integer and the tie breaks. Watch the peak move on the

items.page: Random Variables: Mapping Outcomes to Numbers
items.caption: Normal density: a continuous random variable
items.text: A continuous random variable spreads its probability along the line, so it is described by a density curve and the probability of any exact value is zero; a discrete variable would be described by separate bars instead. The area under this bell is 1. Toggle between the density and its CDF on the

items.page: Law of Total Probability: Weighted Case Analysis
items.caption: Event A drawn across a three-compartment partition
items.text: The Venn view of the same idea: the partition slices the sample space into compartments, event A cuts across all of them, and the probability of A is the sum of its pieces inside each compartment. The tree and the table show the same sum in other shapes. Select a compartment and read the piece of A inside it on the

items.secTitle: Tree Diagrams and the Law of Total Probability
items.caption: One outcome highlighted across every branch
items.text: The first-level branches are the disjoint cases of the law of total probability, and the highlighted outcome appears once in each; its overall probability is the sum of the path products leading to it. The tree makes the partition and the sum visible at once. Highlight an outcome and add its paths on the

items.secTitle: Using Tree Diagrams to Compute Probabilities
items.caption: One complete path: multiply along the branches
items.text: A complete path is one sequence of outcomes, and its probability is the product of the branch weights along it, here P(A) times P(B given A). Adding the products of several paths gives the probability of any event made of those sequences. Follow other paths and multiply on the

items.caption: A dataset around its mean of 20
items.text: Variance measures how far the points scatter around the mean: each deviation is squared and the squares are averaged, so points far from 20 count far more than points near it. items.caption: Standard normal density
items.text: The bell curve is the most used continuous family: symmetric about its mean, with a spread set by the standard deviation and tails that fall off quickly. The exponential and uniform families in the same explorer show a skewed and a flat alternative. Change the parameters and watch the bell move and widen on the

items.caption: Exponential CDF, lambda = 1
items.text: Calculations with a continuous distribution go through the CDF: the probability of an interval is F at its right end minus F at its left end, so the area under the density never has to be integrated by hand once F is known. For the exponential family F(x) equals 1 minus e to the minus lambda x, which the curve traces. Pick an interval and read the difference on the

items.text: A discrete distribution lives on separate values: six bars stand at 1 through 6, each of height 1/6, and there is nothing in between because the variable cannot land there. items.caption: Exponential density, lambda = 1
items.text: The density starts at height lambda at zero and decays geometrically: short waiting times are the most likely and long ones become rare at a constant relative rate. The area under the whole curve is 1 although the curve never touches the axis. Change lambda and watch the starting height and the decay trade off on the

items.caption: Exponential CDF, lambda = 1
items.text: The cumulative probability rises fastest at zero and flattens toward 1, mirroring the decaying density above it; F(x) is 1 minus e to the minus lambda x, so the median sits where the curve crosses one half. The gap between the curve and 1 is the survival probability that drives the memoryless property. Read the probability of waiting at most x on the

items.page: Normal Distribution: Bell Curve, PDF & Z-Scores
items.caption: Normal density, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: The bell is symmetric about the mean, peaks there at about 0.4 for unit standard deviation, and has inflection points one standard deviation to each side. The total area is 1, with about 68 percent of it inside one standard deviation of the mean. Change the parameters and see the bell shift and stretch on the

items.page: Normal Distribution: Bell Curve, PDF & Z-Scores
items.caption: Normal CDF, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: The S-curve passes through one half at the mean and approaches 0 and 1 in the tails; its slope at any point is the density there, which is why it is steepest at the centre. Values are read from tables or software because the integral has no elementary form. Move along the curve and read cumulative probabilities on the

items.page: Probability Inequalities: Bounds Without Full Distributions
items.caption: Chebyshev bound for a normal variable, mean 10, variance 4, deviation 3
items.text: The shaded tails are the actual probability of straying at least 3 from the mean and the bound is variance over 9, which sits well above them: the inequality is valid but loose because it uses only the variance. The Markov visualizer shows the even looser bound that uses only the mean. Change the deviation and compare bound and truth on the

items.caption: Chebyshev bound for a normal variable, mean 10, variance 4, deviation 3
items.text: The bound is the variance divided by the square of the deviation, here 4 over 9, and the shaded tails show the true probability of deviating by at least 3, which is much smaller. Two units of standard deviation against a deviation of three produces the same ratio for every distribution. Change the variance or the deviation and watch the bound move on the

items.caption: Chebyshev bound for a uniform variable
items.text: For a uniform variable the true tail probability can be zero while the bound stays positive: the inequality knows only the variance and cannot see that the distribution has no tails at all. That gap is the price of generality. Switch between families and see how loose the bound gets on the

items.caption: Markov bound for an exponential variable, mean 10, threshold 15
items.text: The bound is the mean over the threshold, 10 over 15, and the shaded tail is the true probability of exceeding 15, which for the exponential family is e to the minus 1.5, about 0.22. The inequality holds for any non-negative variable with that mean, whatever its shape. Slide the threshold and watch bound and tail move on the

items.caption: A threshold below the mean: the bound exceeds 1 and says nothing
items.text: When the threshold is smaller than the mean the ratio is larger than 1, and a probability bound above 1 carries no information. Even for thresholds above the mean the bound is usually far from the truth because it ignores everything except the expected value. Move the threshold across the mean and watch the bound become useless on the

items.page: Probability Function: PMF and PDF Explained
items.caption: Normal density, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: The density function has no bars: its height at a point is not a probability, and only the area under the curve over an interval is. The total area is 1 and the peak at the mean is about 0.4 for unit standard deviation. Toggle to the CDF view and watch the area become a height on the

items.caption: Normal density, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: Density is probability per unit length: the curve is highest at the mean, where a small interval captures the most probability, and the probability of any interval is the area above it. The height 0.4 at the centre is not itself a probability. Toggle to the CDF view and see the accumulated area on the

items.caption: Normal CDF, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: The CDF is the running area under the density, so its slope at any point is the density there: the S-curve is steepest at the mean where the bell is highest and flattens in the tails where the bell is low. Differentiating F recovers f and integrating f recovers F. Move along the curve and compare slope with density on the

items.caption: Exponential density, lambda = 1, with the mean marked
items.text: The catalogue of continuous densities includes this decaying curve for waiting times, the flat uniform density and the normal bell; each is a different rule for spreading unit area over the line. The explorer marks the mean on each, here at 1 over lambda. Compare the three shapes and their parameters on the

items.caption: Continuous uniform, a = 0 to b = 10
items.text: A straight line of slope 0.1 between the bounds, flat at 0 before a and flat at 1 after b. F(5) = 0.5 exactly, and the slope of the line is the density 1/(b-a).

items.secTitle: Normal: the S-Curve and the 68-95-99.7 Rule
items.caption: Normal, mean 0, standard deviation 1
items.text: The sigmoid, symmetric about the mean: F(0) = 0.5, F(1) = 0.8413, F(-1) = 0.1587. Their difference, 0.6827, is the 68% of the empirical rule.

items.caption: Exponential, lambda = 1
items.text: A fast rise then a long flattening: F(1) = 0.6321 at one mean lifetime, and the right edge of the window is still only 0.9931. The median, ln2 = 0.6931, sits left of the mean.

items.caption: Discrete uniform, a = 1 to b = 6
items.text: Six bars of identical height 1/6 = 0.1667 summing to exactly 1. No peak, so every value is a mode - and the mean, 3.5, is not one of the six possible outcomes.

items.secTitle: Normal: the Bell and the Sigmoid
items.caption: Normal, mean 0, sigma 1: PDF above, CDF below
items.text: The bell peaks at 1/sqrt(2 pi) = 0.3989 and the sigmoid crosses 0.5 at the mean. Shrink sigma and the peak rises without limit - a density may exceed 1, a probability may not.

items.secTitle: Exponential: Peak at Zero, Tail Without End
items.caption: Exponential, lambda = 1: PDF above, CDF below
items.text: Density is largest at the very edge of the support, f(0) = 1, with no interior peak. The plotted CDF ends at 0.9931 - the remaining 0.69% lies past the right edge of the window.

items.secTitle: Selecting a Compartment: Conditioning as Restriction

items.text: The ellipse fades and only the part inside B2 stays solid. P(A|B2) = 0.32 / (1/3) = 0.96 - conditioning redraws the frame, so A now fills 96% of a smaller world.

items.secTitle: The Explorer at Its Opening Parameters
items.caption: Normal, mu = 0, sigma = 1: PDF above, CDF below
items.text: The bell peaks at 1/sqrt(2 pi) = 0.3989 and the sigmoid below crosses 0.5 at the mean. Shrink sigma and the peak rises without limit: a density may exceed 1, a probability may not.

items.secTitle: The Explorer at Its Opening Parameter
items.caption: Exponential, lambda = 1: PDF above, CDF below
items.text: Density is largest at the very edge of the support, f(0) = 1, with no interior peak. The window ends at -ln(0.001) = 6.908, so the CDF below stops at exactly 0.999 by construction.

items.secTitle: The Explorer at Its Opening Bounds
items.caption: Continuous uniform, a = 0, b = 10: PDF above, CDF below
items.text: A flat density of 0.1 and a straight-line CDF of slope 0.1. The CDF's slope IS the PDF's height, and its two kinks are where the density jumps from 0 to 0.1 and back.

items.secTitle: Normal: the Bound Against a Bell Curve
items.caption: Normal, E[X] = 10, a = 15
items.text: The curve is the normal restricted to x >= 0 with sigma = 5. The shaded tail is 15.9% against a bound of 66.7% - about four times the truth.

items.secTitle: Exponential: Where Markov Is Tightest Among the Continuous Options
items.caption: Exponential, E[X] = 10, a = 15
items.text: The tool opens here. The tail is exp(-1.5) = 22.3%, the tightest of the three continuous options against the same 66.7% bound.

items.secTitle: Uniform: the Largest Tail of the Nine
items.caption: Uniform on [0, 20], a = 15
items.text: A flat density of 0.05, so the shaded tail is the rectangle from 15 to 20: 5 x 0.05 = 25.0%. The one state whose tail can be checked by hand.

items.secTitle: Poisson: a Discrete Tail Read as Stems
items.caption: Poisson, lambda = 10, a = 15
items.text: The chart switches to stems, and the tool sums the red ones rather than integrating: 8.3%. Poisson mass sits within a few sigma of lambda, and sigma here is only 3.2.

items.caption: Exponential with a = 8, below E[X] = 10
items.text: With a under the mean the bound is 10/8 = 1.25, and the tool turns its header panel red. A bound of 125% is true but empty: every probability is at most 1 anyway.

items.secTitle: Normal: the Bound at Its Most Familiar
items.caption: Normal, mu = 10, sigma^2 = 4, a = 3
items.text: The variance slider does set sigma here, so sigma = 2 and a = 1.5 sigma. Bound 44.4%, actual 13.4% - about as tight as Chebyshev gets.

items.secTitle: Exponential: When the Bound Says Nothing
items.caption: Exponential, lambda = 0.1
items.text: One parameter, so the mean fixes sigma^2 = mu^2 = 100 and the slider does nothing. a = 3 is only 0.3 sigma, so the bound caps at 100% and says nothing; the actual is 77.6%.

items.secTitle: Continuous Uniform: the Other Slider-Driven Case
items.caption: Continuous uniform on [6.54, 13.46]
items.text: Built to have exactly the requested variance, so bound 44.4% and actual 13.4% - identical to the normal at this k, but beyond k = sqrt(3) its actual drops to exactly zero.

items.secTitle: Poisson: Variance Fixed by the Mean
items.caption: Poisson, lambda = 10
items.text: Mean and variance are the same parameter, so sigma^2 = 10 whatever the slider says. a = 3 is 0.95 sigma - just short of one - so the bound is still vacuous. Actual 26.5%.

items.secTitle: Geometric: the Widest Spread on the Page
items.caption: Geometric, p = 0.1
items.text: sigma^2 = 90, nearly the square of the mean. a = 0.32 sigma, bound vacuous, actual 71.6%. The window holds about 99.3% of the mass, so that actual slightly undercounts.

items.caption: Negative binomial, r = 5, p = 1/3
items.text: sigma^2 = 30, between the geometric 90 and the binomial 6 - five waits concentrate more than one, less than twenty-five fixed trials. Actual 51.8%.

items.secTitle: Discrete Uniform: Spread Without a Tail
items.caption: Discrete uniform on 1..19
items.text: Twelve of the nineteen values lie outside [7, 13], so the actual is exactly 12/19 = 63.2%. Same variance as the negative binomial, reached by spreading evenly rather than by a tail.

items.secTitle: Why Four Constraints Are Needed, Not Two
items.caption: Region 1 selected: the triple intersection
items.text: Eight regions need eight equations. Three marginals and the total give four; without four constraints the answer is not unique. With P(B n C) = 0.38 but no value for region 1, any triple intersection from 0.08 to 0.10 fits - the given 0.08 picks one out.
